AI에게 같은 일을 시켜 코드 여러 개를 받았다고 하자. 어느 코드를 써: Suppose AI produces several programs for the same task. Which should we use? If the answer can be determined in advance, run each program and compare its output with that answer. Once the answer is known, a computer can perform the comparison for every new program. AI coding research has used this to select candidates and train models on the results. Whether the same approach works elsewhere depends on what must be checked anew for each answer.
8.4.1 한 번 구한 답으로 수정 전후를 확인한다: 8.4.1 Reuse one known answer to check before and after an edit
종이에 6, 8, 1을 한 줄로 적고 그 아래에도 6, 8, 1을 적어: Write 6, 8, 1 on one line and again below it. Listing each number common to both lines once, in ascending order, gives <v0/>. This example appears in EvalPlus, a study evaluating AI-generated code. The researchers supplied the two lists to ChatGPT-generated code, which returned <v1/>. All three required numbers are present, but the order is wrong from the first position. <v2>Liu et al., EvalPlus, 2023, Figure 1</v2>
어디서 순서가 바뀌었을까? 코드는 공통 숫자를 한 번씩 골라 작은 수부터: Where did the order change? The code selected unique common numbers and sorted them. Just before the last line, <v0/> contained <v1/>. In the final line, <v2/>, the inner <v3/> executes first. A set retains which numbers are present, but not their original positions. The outer <v4/> constructs a new list in the set’s iteration order. When the author ran this code, that order was 8, 1, 6, so the new list was <v5/>. <v6>Python 3.12, set types</v6>
마지막 줄을 <v0/>로 바꾸면 이미 작은 수부터 놓아 둔 목록이 그대로: Replacing the last line with <v0/> returns the already sorted list unchanged. Supply the same two lists again and compare with the known answer. The table calls this answer the “expected value.” Its last two columns show the author’s reruns of the original and revised code on identical inputs. If one input is empty (<v1/>), no numbers occur in both, so the expected result is also an empty list. The first three checks came from the original problem; EvalPlus added the fourth.
표의 둘째 행도 읽어 보자. <v0/>과 <v1/>에는 2와 3이 모두: Consider the second row. Both <v0/> and <v1/> contain 2 and 3, so the ascending result <v2/> is expected. Both versions returned that answer and passed. Across two versions, the four pairs were supplied eight times, but only four reference answers were needed.
둘째 행을 비롯한 처음 세 검사는 원래 코드도 통과했다. 두 코드의 차이: The original code also passed the first three checks, including the second row. The fourth exposed the difference: the original returned the wrong order, while the revised code returned the expected value. Tests can be repeated indefinitely, but their coverage depends on the inputs chosen.
8.4.2 같은 검사로 여러 코드 중에서 고른다: 8.4.2 Use the same checks to choose among programs
앞에서는 코드를 고치기 전후에 같은 검사를 썼다. 같은 정렬 문제를 푸는: The same checks compared code before and after a revision. Those four checks can also evaluate several newly generated programs for the same sorting problem. Their ways of finding common numbers may differ, but the correct result for the two lists remains the same. A computer can run all candidates and compare their outputs to identify those producing the expected results.
구글 딥마인드 연구진은 코딩 AI인 AlphaCode에 대회 문제 하나를: Google DeepMind researchers gave AlphaCode a programming-contest problem and generated many candidate solutions. They allowed at most ten submissions per problem for final judging. Every incorrect submission consumed one opportunity, so they studied which selection strategy solved more problems within that limit.
한 방법에서는 만들어 둔 코드 전체에서 무작위로 골랐다. 다른 방법에서는: One strategy selected randomly from all generated programs. Another first ran each program on examples from the problem, retained only those producing the example answers, and selected randomly from that subset. Both strategies were judged using separate, undisclosed tests. A problem counted as solved if any submitted program passed all those tests. <v0>Li et al., AlphaCode, 2022, Figure 8</v0>
두 방법에서 코드 수와 제출 한도는 같았다. 후보가 충분할 때는 예시 검: Candidate counts and submission limits were identical. With enough candidates, filtering by example tests first solved more problems, removing demonstrably wrong programs before final judging. Reusing checks to eliminate incorrect candidates makes better use of limited submission opportunities.
8.4.3 검사 결과로 AI를 훈련하고 새 모델을 비교한다: 8.4.3 Use test results to train AI and compare models
코드가 틀렸다는 판정도 AI를 훈련할 때는 점수가 된다. CodeRL 연: A verdict that code is wrong can itself become a training score. CodeRL executed AI-generated code and assigned different scores to different outcomes, including compilation errors and runtime errors. Code that finished but failed tests received −0.3; code passing every test received 1. The researchers used these scores to train AI to produce passing code more often. <v0>Le et al., CodeRL, 2022, scores by execution outcome</v0>
Collecting training scores requires grading each new program. Once the scoring rules are defined, a computer assigns scores from execution outcomes, reducing the need for a person to read and judge every program. If tests finish quickly, results from many attempts can keep feeding training.
훈련 방법을 바꾼 뒤에는 AI가 전보다 잘 푸는지도 확인해야 한다. Op: After changing training methods, researchers must check whether AI solves more problems. OpenAI’s HumanEval contains 164 human-written programming problems with executable tests. Giving models before and after training the same problems and the same number of attempts lets researchers compare how many pass. Their code may differ line by line, but the evaluation criterion remains the same. Identifying which problems changed provides evidence for choosing the next training method. <v0>Chen et al., HumanEval, 2021, evaluation method</v0>
AI 연구자 안드레이 카파시는 AI가 여러 번 연습하기 좋은 조건을 설명: AI researcher Andrej Karpathy described conditions favorable to repeated AI practice: the same starting conditions, low time and cost for another attempt, and automatic grading. The sorting example immediately reuses the same two lists and compares output with expected values. Whether web answers or slides can likewise be graded automatically depends on what must be judged for each new result. <v0/>
8.4.4 다른 분야에서도 답을 한 번 정해 두고 채점할 수 있을까: 8.4.4 Can other fields also grade against a predefined answer?
인터넷에서 찾는 데 오래 걸리는 답도 비교할 답을 미리 마련하면 채점하기: Even a fact that takes a long time to find online can be easy to grade if a reference answer is prepared. OpenAI’s BrowseComp evaluates web search with hard-to-find facts and short researcher-prepared answers. After the searching AI returns an answer, a grading AI checks whether its meaning matches the reference. Sorting checks identical numbers at identical positions; web answers may use different wording, so semantic equivalence is checked. Both reuse the same reference for each new answer. <v0>Wei et al., BrowseComp, 2025, grading method</v0>
BrowseComp가 이런 방식으로 채점할 수 있었던 데에는 질문을 만드: The order of question construction made this possible in BrowseComp. Researchers asked question writers to choose a fact first, then construct a question making that fact difficult to discover. Because the target answer is fixed, even a long search can end in a direct comparison. Within the same field, question design changes the effort required to verify results. <v0>Wei et al., BrowseComp, 2025, question construction</v0>
발표 자료를 비교할 때는 새 초안마다 판단할 일이 남는다. 정렬 예제의: Comparing presentations leaves new judgments for every draft. The sorting example’s fourth check simply compares with the predefined <v0/>. But the same presentation request can yield different structures and explanations. Each draft needs review for required content and readable layout. In OpenAI’s GDPval study, experienced professionals read the request and reference materials and compared deliverables without knowing who produced them. On public tasks, one expert comparison took more than an hour on average. <v1>OpenAI, GDPval, 2025, expert and automated grading</v1>

For example, an agent asked to summarize a page may execute malicious instructions embedded in it. (<v1/>) This section examines how <v2>prompt injection</v2> and tool poisoning distort coding-agent behavior. It first explains why agents follow external instructions and identifies the external inputs and risks encountered during work. 1. AI는 왜 외부 자료에 포함된 지시를 따르는가?: 1. Why does AI follow instructions embedded in external material?
LLM 기반 코딩 에이전트는 대화형 챗봇과 달리, 저장소 파일이나 웹 검: Unlike a conversational chatbot, an LLM-based coding agent works by reading and processing varied text, including repository files and web results. Unlike conventional software, however, <v0>an LLM does not distinguish instructions from ordinary data</v0>. Any text can potentially be interpreted as a prompt, so an agent may mistake malicious instructions in retrieved material for legitimate directions. Instructions hidden in data can therefore be acted on even when they did not come from the user. OWASP calls malicious instructions in directly supplied input <v1>direct prompt injection (Direct PI)</v1>, and attacks using hidden instructions in retrieved external material <v2>indirect prompt injection (Indirect PI)</v2>. (<v3/>) An attacker’s instructions in a page or repository file may function like system or user instructions when the agent reads them.
기존 소프트웨어는 일반적으로 코드와 데이터를 엄격히 분리하여, 코드 흐름: Conventional software generally separates code and data to prevent data from changing control flow. LLM agents instead treat configuration files such as <v0/> and <v1/>, README files, and even tool descriptions as text that can become instructions depending on context. An unofficial, unreviewed research note from the Cloud Security Alliance AI Safety Initiative says major coding tools, including GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code, automatically load repository configuration files into initial context and trust them at nearly system-prompt level. (<v2/>) This architecture offers no guarantee that agents can identify legitimate directions. As the warning “a repository is not a trust boundary” suggests, treating repository files as trusted information may have suited human readers but does not safely transfer to LLM agents.
결국 에이전트는 일반 텍스트 형식의 외부 데이터를 명령어로 오인하여 실행: Agents can therefore mistake plain-text external data for instructions and act on it, because no clear boundary separates the user’s original request from commands mixed into that data. Greshake and colleagues (2023) argued that LLM-integrated applications blur the data-instruction boundary. (<v0/>) Debenedetti and colleagues’ AgentDojo study (2024) likewise explains that direct text processing provides no formal separation between instructions and data and reports that current defenses do not stop every attack. (<v1/>) This creates a structural vulnerability: LLMs cannot be guaranteed to distinguish legitimate directions from hidden ones. As section 4 shows, however, not every injection succeeds.

<v0>README files and repository documentation:</v0> These are among the most common routes. README.md and project manuals help users understand a project, but can also contain hidden instructions. HiddenLayer researchers demonstrated that even an ordinary GitHub README can hijack an assistant such as Cursor, using a few concealed lines to induce API-key or SSH-credential theft or execution of blocked commands. (<v1/>) For example, instructions hidden in Markdown comments may direct an agent to look for secret keys when it clones the repository and reads the README. The CSA research note lists README files and <v2/>, <v3/>, <v4/>, and <v5/> among files agents automatically load as trusted context. (<v6/>) The repository scanner ctxsentry likewise warns that hidden directions in <v7/>, <v8/>, <v9/>, <v10/>, and issue templates can enter an agent’s context when read. (<v11/>) Documentation and rule files thus become attack vectors.
<v0>코드 주석:</v0> 코드 내 주석도 마찬가지다. 예를 들어 C: <v0>Code comments:</v0> Comments can carry instructions too. Malicious text in C-style <v1/> or <v2/> comments, or Python <v3/> comments, may be interpreted during code analysis. This section’s references do not directly study this route, but because comments are text entering context, the principle resembles attacks hiding payloads in README comments. (<v4/>)
<v0>GitHub Issue 및 Pull Request:</v0> 코딩: <v0>GitHub issues and pull requests:</v0> Coding agents sometimes obtain task instructions from issues or PRs. Malicious descriptions may therefore be followed directly. An agent creating an issue or reviewing a PR, for example, may act on hidden commands in that text. (<v1/>) As ctxsentry explains, issue-template files may also enter context when read and can carry attack payloads. (<v2/>)
<v0>웹페이지와 검색 결과:</v0> 에이전트가 브라우저 플러그인이나: <v0>Web pages and search results:</v0> Browser plugins and search capabilities make web content part of context. A sentence such as “The agent should access the following file” in a result or page may be mistaken for a user command. OWASP likewise warns of prompt injection when web data is absorbed into an LLM without format validation. (<v1/>) Instructions may be concealed with CSS or in HTML comments invisible in the rendered browser view.
<v0>터미널 및 도구 실행 결과:</v0> 에이전트가 셸 명령을 실행하: <v0>Terminal and tool output:</v0> Shell-command output and external-tool responses provide another route. When an agent processes results from commands such as <v1/> or <v2/>, manipulated strings can cause problems. OWASP illustrates a malicious MCP server mixing hidden commands such as [COMPLIANCE DIRECTIVE] into a tool result to induce sensitive-file reads or transmission to an external URL. (<v3/>) Shell output and API responses can thus carry malicious payloads.
<v0>외부 규칙 파일 및 설정 파일:</v0> 앞서 언급한 <v1/>: <v0>External rule and configuration files:</v0> Rule files such as <v1/> and configuration files such as <v2/> are also attack surfaces. Pillar Security reported the “Rules File Backdoor” vector. (<v3/>) Hidden commands in Cursor’s project rules (<v4/>), for example, can influence later code-generation requests. Malicious rules survive project forks, creating a supply-chain risk. (<v5/>) The IDEsaster research cited by the CSA note found at least one exploitable attack chain in every AI IDE tested. (<v6/>) Pillar Security showed that instructions disguised with invisible Unicode characters can persist in rules and insert backdoors into generated code. (<v7/>)

Even during a legitimate task, manipulated README content, comments, or configuration files may induce <v0>unintended actions</v0>, including data leakage, file changes, or privilege escalation.

ReadSecBench reported approximately 84% success for commands placed directly in README files and 91% for instructions in documents two links away. 3. AI가 사용하는 도구 자체를 신뢰할 수 있을까?: 3. Can we trust the tools AI uses?
바이브 코딩 에이전트는 코드 편집 도구, 셸, 브라우저 등 다양한 <v0: Vibe coding agents call various <v0>external tools</v0>, including editors, shells, and browsers. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standardized tool interface. (<v1/>) It lets agents connect tool servers that supply names, descriptions, and input schemas. But descriptions and returned responses also enter LLM context directly. These external inputs can therefore act as instructions.
<v0>도구 설명의 오염 (Description Poisoning):</: <v0>Description poisoning:</v0> An attacker can operate an MCP server presenting ordinary tool names and apparently legitimate descriptions while embedding hidden instructions in the descriptive text. Invariant Labs demonstrated an addition tool resembling <v1/> with instructions such as reading SSH keys hidden in <v2/> tags. Although the user wanted only addition, the LLM read the hidden directions and accessed sensitive files such as <v3/>. This is commonly called <v4>tool poisoning</v4>. (<v5/>) Users may inspect a description once, but agents consult the actual contents, including code and commands, during execution. Once trust is granted, an attacker may later change the description without the agent critically reassessing it. (<v6/>)
<v0>도구 응답의 오염 (Response Poisoning):</v0>: <v0>Response poisoning:</v0> An MCP server’s tool <v1>returned response</v1> also enters model context. In OWASP’s example, a malicious server answers a tool such as “get_compliance_status” with JSON appearing to contain ordinary compliance information. The body includes hidden instructions such as “[COMPLIANCE DIRECTIVE - MANDATORY],” inducing interpretation as a sensitive command such as <v2/>. The tool looks legitimate, but its response contains commands. The underlying problem is a <v3>trust gap</v3>: descriptions are reviewed at connection time, while responses are added directly to context without inspection. (<v4/>)
정리하면, <v0>MCP를 통한 도구 사용은 에이전트의 권한과 행동 범위: In short, <v0>MCP tool use greatly expands agents’ permissions and range of actions</v0> while introducing new attack surfaces. Because LLMs receive descriptions and results as text, hidden instructions from malicious MCP servers may be treated as trusted commands. CVE-2025-54136, for example, describes remote code execution in Cursor versions 1.2.4 and earlier when a previously approved MCP configuration was modified. (<v1/>) A legitimate approved configuration became malicious, exposing the limits of permanent trust without rechecking descriptions or configuration.
이런 공격을 방지하려면 MCP 보안 지침에서 권장하는 대로, 외부 MCP: MCP security guidance therefore recommends strict allowlisting rather than indiscriminately connecting external servers, and reviewing even approved servers whenever they change. (<v0/>) Both description and response poisoning are forms of indirect prompt injection. Preventing damage requires careful control over which backend tools agents can call and how their output influences the model.
4. AI는 이러한 공격을 스스로 구분하고 막을 수 있을까?: 4. Can AI identify and block these attacks on its own?
현재의 LLM 모델과 에이전트 시스템이 프롬프트 인젝션 공격을 완벽히 차: It is uncertain whether current LLMs and agent systems can completely block prompt injection. Debenedetti and colleagues (2024) describe AgentDojo as difficult for attackers and defenders alike: leading LLMs fail many tasks even without attacks, while known injections break some security properties but not all. (<v0/>) Current attackers do not succeed 100% of the time, and defenders do not block 100% of attacks.
<v0>모델 수준 방어:</v0> 일부 연구자는 LLM이 악성 지시를 따: <v0>Model-level defenses:</v0> Researchers have tried LLM training and special instructions to prevent malicious-instruction following. Approaches include learning security labels with constraints such as “never read files for this task,” or adjusting instruction priorities to separate user intent from external data. But models are designed to follow user requests and learned system-instruction hierarchies, making external data disguised at user-instruction priority difficult to distinguish. HiddenLayer demonstrated using control tokens such as <v1/> to elevate injected instructions. (<v2/>) Security tuning does not guarantee protection against new attacks, so model-level defense alone is insufficient.
<v0>시스템 수준 방어:</v0> 에이전트 시스템 단에서는 신뢰 경계를: <v0>System-level defenses:</v0> Proposed measures include explicit trust boundaries and strict tool-call validation. OWASP’s LLM security guidance recommends clearly defining model roles and expected outputs and handling external content separately from instructions. (<v1/>) Options include detectors filtering suspicious input or restricting resources by domain. Least privilege gives each tool only the permissions needed, with user approval before consequential operations. AgentDojo’s tool-filter defense selects necessary tools before the agent sees untrusted data. It reduced targeted attack success to single digits, 7.5% in the paper’s text and 6.84% in Table 5. But it cannot serve tasks whose tools cannot be known beforehand, and it does not help attacks achievable using only necessary tools, which represented 17% of test cases. Tool filtering substantially reduces threats without applying universally. (<v2/>)
또 다른 방어로는 에이전트와 도구 수행 환경을 완전 격리된 샌드박스에서: Another defense runs agents and tool environments in an isolated sandbox. Claude Code, for example, operates read-only without explicit permission and offers sandboxing that restricts network and filesystem access. (<v0/>) GitHub Copilot CLI and the Copilot app likewise offer local sandboxes controlling commands’ filesystem and network permissions. (<v1/>) These system defenses focus on containing damage even when injection succeeds, rather than solely detecting injection itself.
요약하면, 최신 연구들은 다양한 방어 메커니즘을 제안했지만 아직 한계가: Recent research therefore proposes varied defenses but still finds substantial limits. In AgentDojo, <v0>repeating the user prompt</v0> achieved the highest normal-task utility, 85.53% versus 69.0% without defense, but targeted attack success remained 27.82%. The authors expected it to struggle against adaptive attacks. <v1>Tool filtering</v1> further reduces attack success but has the applicability limits discussed above. (<v2/>) Complete defense would require complex system design, while excessive restrictions reduce usefulness. The practical approach is layered defense combining agent-level security modules with backend permission management.
5. 바이브 코딩 사용자는 어떻게 자신을 보호할 수 있을까?: 5. How can vibe coding users protect themselves?
위에서 설명한 위험과 제한적인 방어 연구들을 바탕으로, 실제 바이브 코딩: Based on the risks and limited defense research above, users can take practical measures in real vibe coding environments. These fall broadly into environment preparation, permission management, and review of code and tools.
<v0>샌드박스 환경 활용:</v0> 에이전트를 분리된 격리 공간에서 실: <v0>Use a sandbox:</v0> Run the agent in a separate, isolated space. Claude Code sandboxing, for example, lets users predefine accessible directories and network hosts and prevent the agent from leaving those boundaries. (<v1/>) Both filesystem and network isolation are necessary. GitHub Copilot CLI and the Copilot app also support local sandboxes, disabled by default. Without enabling them, agents can access files and networks using the user account’s permissions. (<v2/>) Run tool calls inside a sandbox or container whenever possible to prevent external leakage.
<v0>최소 권한 원칙 준수:</v0> 에이전트에 과도한 권한을 부여하지: <v0>Apply least privilege:</v0> Avoid excessive permissions. In AWS, use temporary credentials through IAM roles and policies granting only what the task requires. If an agent only needs to read a particular S3 bucket, for example, grant <v1/> and <v2/> and prohibit other operations. In general, issue disposable tokens or restricted API keys and avoid hardcoding credentials such as access keys. (<v3/>)
<v0>파일 및 저장소 접근 범위 제한:</v0> 에이전트가 읽거나 변경: <v0>Limit file and repository access:</v0> Narrow the scope agents can read or modify. With Copilot CLI sandboxing enabled, users can specify readable and writable paths and allow only necessary network hosts. (<v1/>) Claude Code sandboxing can likewise block file access outside the current working directory. (<v2/>) Manage public repositories separately from private repositories containing sensitive data, and keep internal code and configuration separate from public projects where possible.
<v0>민감 정보와 인증정보 보호:</v0> 프롬프트나 코드 안에 API: <v0>Protect secrets and credentials:</v0> Never expose API keys, passwords, or SSH private keys in prompts or code. Avoid sharing SSH keys with an agent even in a local sandbox. Manage environment variables and credentials potentially exposed through tool calls using secure stores such as Git Credential Manager or Vault (Secrets Manager), and give the agent only narrowly scoped tokens.
<v0>중요 도구 실행에 대한 사용자 승인:</v0> 에이전트가 코드를: <v0>Require approval for consequential tool execution:</v0> Configure explicit user approval before code changes or command execution. Claude Code’s default mode is designed to grant read-only access and require approval for writes and commands. (<v1/>) Approval and isolation are separate controls, so combine it with sandboxing such as Copilot CLI’s <v2/>. (<v3/>) Minimize the available action list and require confirmation before risky actions, including file deletion and external communication.
<v0>외부 저장소 및 MCP 서버 검증:</v0> 에이전트가 접근할 외: <v0>Verify external repositories and MCP servers:</v0> Check the provenance of resources agents will access. Files in public repositories editable by many people deserve particular review. Verify that added MCP server addresses come from trusted sources and assess the source for malicious content. Where possible, validate external tool lists against fixed formats such as JSON Schema or maintain a server allowlist to prevent unverified connections. (<v1/>)

When reviewing AI changes in a GitHub pull request, for example, check for unusual modifications to Markdown comments or configuration files. Record calls so you can trace when each tool was invoked and what it returned. This history supports incident analysis and response when an attack is suspected.

(<v0/>, <v1/>) Use these capabilities appropriately while recognizing that features and recommended settings can change.

Workflows coordinate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; agents let the LLM determine progress and tool use dynamically.<v0/> Reading workflow code reveals the execution order. With agents, the model chooses tool order during execution, so records are needed to see what it did.

But a model’s step-by-step explanation, or chain of thought, may differ from its actual basis for judgment. Turpin and colleagues biased inputs, for example by always placing example answers at option (A). Models selected incorrect answers because of the bias yet plausibly justified them without mentioning it. Across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks, accuracy fell by up to 36% (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0).<v0/>

Enabling it records tool names by default but not edited file paths or executed commands. 기록을 남긴 다음에는 읽는 방법이 필요하다. Bouzenia와 Prade: Once records exist, we need a way to read them. Bouzenia and Pradel analyzed 120 trajectories from RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover, and OpenHands, containing 2,822 LLM calls, about 24 per trajectory. Reading them verbatim from beginning to end is lengthy. The researchers divided records into thought-action-result groups, classified actions, and identified recurring sequences. The most frequent actions were patch generation (23%), test execution (19%), search (15%), and exploration (14%).<v0/>

The authors identified three inefficient patterns: repeating actions without incorporating their results, generating consecutive patches without testing, and ending without adequate test verification. Looking for these patterns first can narrow down where judgment went wrong.

Zhang and colleagues created Who&When by having people label which agent caused failure at which step in 127 failed LLM multi-agent trajectories. Even the best automatic method identified the responsible agent only 53.5% of the time and the step only 14.2%.<v0/> People still need to read records to pinpoint the mistaken decision.

Both OpenTelemetry conventions and Claude Code disable content recording by default. Decide what to enable by weighing its diagnostic value against the risks of exposure.
